title: Quantifying the Dual-isotope Advantage for Ytterbium-array Surface Codes using Realistic Noise Models
authors: Fumiyoshi Kobayashi, Toshi Kusano, Nicholas Fazio, Yuma Nakamura
abstract: Neutral-atom quantum computers are a promising platform for fault-tolerant quantum computation, but logical performance depends on systemic realistic noise factors during syndrome extraction. In dual-isotope Yb arrays, the roles of data and ancilla qubits are separated spectrally, allowing ancilla qubits to be measured in place without additional transport or shelving operations. Here we quantify the advantage of a dual-isotope Yb architecture for surface code memories. We develop an experimentally motivated Clifford-compatible noise model for dual-isotope 171Yb-174Yb systems using generalised Pauli twirling and implement it as a wrapper for Stim called DualYbSim, which has been packaged as an open source Python library. Simulations of rotated and XZZX surface codes show that a dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement achieves the lowest logical error rates among the architectures considered, outperforming single-isotope schemes based on shelving or zoned measurement. Our error-budget analysis also identifies Rydberg-state decay as the dominant limitation, contributing to 74-80% of the logical error rate scaling, highlighting concrete experimental targets for improving FTQC performance.
summary: This paper analyzes the performance of neutral-atom quantum computers for fault-tolerant quantum computation using Ytterbium isotopes. By developing a realistic noise model, the authors demonstrate that a dual-isotope architecture significantly outperforms single-isotope methods due to efficient in-place measurement. The study provides critical error-budget analysis, identifying Rydberg-state decay as the primary bottleneck for improving future quantum processors.
main_problem: To quantify the advantage of using a dual-isotope Ytterbium architecture for implementing surface codes in fault-tolerant quantum computation (FTQC) compared to single-isotope schemes.
main_result: The dual-isotope architecture with in-place measurement achieves the lowest logical error rates, and the analysis pinpoints Rydberg-state decay as the dominant error source, contributing 74-80% of the logical error rate.
method: The authors developed an experimentally motivated Clifford-compatible noise model using generalized Pauli twirling and simulated surface codes (rotated and XZZX) using an open-source Python library, DualYbSim.
model_or_system: The system uses neutral-atom quantum computers with dual-isotope Yb arrays ($^{171}	ext{Yb}$ and $^{174}	ext{Yb}$). Qubits are encoded in different ground/metastable states, and gates rely on the Rydberg blockade effect. The noise model accounts for various decay and measurement channels.
key_observables: Logical Error Rates (LER) for surface codes, and the contribution of specific noise channels (e.g., Rydberg-state decay) to the total error budget.
important_parameters: The ratio of logical error rates between dual-isotope vs. single-isotope schemes; the decay rate of the Rydberg state.
main_assumptions: The noise model simplifies complex sublevel structures, and the analysis ignores transportation noise associated with qubit replenishment.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the dual-isotope layout for surface code memories. Figure 2 illustrates the syndrome extraction circuits for the surface code and the XZZX stabilizer check.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the challenge of noise in neutral-atom FTQC, details the dual-isotope architecture and its noise model, simulates performance on various surface codes, and concludes with an error-budget analysis identifying key physical limitations.
why_interesting: This work directly tackles the engineering challenges of scaling quantum computation by providing quantitative metrics on architectural advantages (dual-isotope vs. single-isotope) and identifying the dominant physical error sources that must be addressed experimentally.
